How Deep Are Water Lines Buried? A Florida Homeowner's Guide

By SRQ Leak Pros Editorial · Published November 5, 2026 · Updated November 5, 2026 · 7 min read

Short answer: In Florida, water lines are buried shallower than in cold states. A Florida Building Code plumbing supplement sets water service pipe at no less than 12 inches deep. Many Sarasota service lines sit about 12 to 24 inches down, but real depth varies with grading, landscaping and who installed the line. Never assume. Locate it before you dig.

How deep are water lines buried? It's a fair question before you plant a tree, set a fence post or chase a wet spot in the lawn. The answer matters even more when the line is leaking. If yours is, SRQ Leak Pros can connect you with a local provider for water line replacement in Sarasota or a targeted repair.

This guide covers code depths, why your line may not match them, Florida's dig rules and how a pro finds the pipe.

How deep are water lines buried in Florida?

Florida's code minimum for a water service line is 12 inches of cover. The Florida Building Code plumbing supplement places that rule in Section 305.6, the section on freezing. It reads that water service pipe shall be installed not less than 12 inches deep. In colder states the rule ties depth to the frost line, which can push lines several feet down.

Sarasota rarely freezes hard, so lines don't need that much cover. The 12-inch rule protects the pipe from surface loads, lawn work and the odd cold snap. Code editions change, so check the current rule with the Sarasota County or city building department before new work.

Typical depths by part of the system

Part of the systemTypical depthWho usually owns it
Public water main under the streetDeeper than service lines; varies by utilityWater utility
Pipe from the main to the meterShallow, ending at the meter boxWater utility
Service line from the meter to the houseAbout 12 to 24 inches, oftenProperty owner
Irrigation linesOften 6 to 12 inchesProperty owner
Pool plumbingShallow runs near the deckProperty owner

These are field ranges, not guarantees. Depths change along one run. A line can rise near the meter box, dip under a walkway and come up again at the house wall.

Why your water line may not match the code

Real depth often drifts from the plan. Common reasons:

  • Regrading. Soil was added or scraped away after the line went in.
  • Landscaping. Raised beds, mulch and sod change the cover.
  • Erosion. Heavy rain and sandy soil wash cover away near slopes and drains.
  • Old installs. Older lines may have gone in shallower than today's code.
  • Repairs. A past fix may have rerouted part of the line.
  • Driveways and pavers. Base material can sit right on top of the pipe.

The only way to know is to locate the line on your own lot.

Do I need to call 811 before digging in Florida?

Yes, in most cases. Florida requires a call to Sunshine 811 at least two full business days before you dig. Member utilities then mark their buried lines, such as gas, power and cable.

There's a narrow homeowner exemption. Florida Statutes § 556.108 lets the owner of a single-family home dig on their own land without notice only to a depth of 10 inches. The owner must use due care and can't dig into a utility's right-of-way or easement. Since a water line may sit only 12 inches down, a 10-inch hole leaves very little room for error.

Does 811 mark my water line?

Not usually the part you own. Sunshine 811 sends notice to member utilities, and each marks its own lines. The pipe from your meter to the house, your sprinkler lines and your pool plumbing belong to you. Those private lines are generally not part of the utility marks. That's why many owners hire a pro to trace them.

How do pros find a buried water line?

A provider uses one or more of these methods:

  1. Start at known points. The meter box and the spot where the pipe enters the house mark both ends.
  2. Line tracing. A transmitter puts a signal on metal pipe or on a trace wire, and a receiver follows it across the yard.
  3. Sonde or push rod. For plastic pipe with no wire, a small transmitter can be pushed inside the line in some cases.
  4. Acoustic listening. If the line is leaking, ground microphones detect the sound of escaping water.
  5. Pot-holing. A small, careful hole by hand or vacuum confirms the exact depth before heavy digging.

Plastic pipe is harder to trace than copper. If your service line is PVC, PEX or polybutylene with no wire, expect more time on locating. Our guide on how to locate underground water lines covers each method in more detail.

Does depth change the repair cost?

Yes. Deeper or harder-to-reach pipe means more digging, more restoration and more time. Angi's national data puts the average main water line replacement at about $1,710, or about $50 to $250 per linear foot. Shallow lines under open lawn sit at the low end. Lines under driveways, pavers or pools cost more to reach. A trenchless bore can avoid tearing up the surface. See trenchless water line replacement for how that works.

Florida rules on who can work on a service line

Florida places work on water service lines within the scope of a plumbing contractor. Section 489.105(3)(m) of the Florida Statutes covers installing and repairing water lines from the meter to the building. Hire a licensed plumbing contractor for the repair, and check the license on the DBPR site. A permit and inspection are often needed for a new line.

Sarasota yards and shallow water lines

Sarasota's sandy soil digs easily, which cuts both ways. A shovel goes deep fast, so it's easy to reach a shallow pipe without meaning to. Coastal lots can also have a high water table, which fills holes with water and hides the pipe.

Many homes here also have long irrigation runs crossing the service line. A shallow sprinkler pipe can look like the main line at first glance. Check the size and color, or ask a pro to confirm.

Sarasota County notes that it maintains more than 104,000 service lines. Its staff check reported leaks and decide whether the problem sits on the county's side or the customer's.

How to dig safely near a water line

  • Call Sunshine 811 first, even for small jobs.
  • Find the meter box and the house entry point.
  • Mark a likely path between them before you start.
  • Use a hand shovel near the marked path, not a power auger.
  • Stop at about 10 inches unless you have marks and a plan.
  • If you hit water, shut off the main and don't keep digging.

Local note: many newer lots in Lakewood Ranch have deep landscaping beds over the line. Older Venice homes may have lines that were repaired or rerouted over the years. On Siesta Key, a high water table can make even a shallow hole fill fast.

When should you call a water line professional?

Call a pro when:

  • You need to dig near the line and can't find it
  • A wet spot, sinkhole or soggy patch shows up between the meter and the house
  • You nicked or broke a pipe while digging
  • Your line is old and you're weighing repair or replacement

Frequently asked questions

How deep is a water main under the street?

Public water mains usually sit deeper than home service lines, but depth varies by utility and street. Call Sunshine 811 so the utility can mark its lines before you dig.

Can a water line be too shallow?

Yes. A line with little cover can be damaged by lawn work, vehicles or heat. If yours is shallow, a pro can lower it, add protection or reroute it.

How deep are irrigation lines usually buried?

Sprinkler lines are often shallower than the service line, commonly 6 to 12 inches. They can still crack under a shovel.

Is it safe to dig 10 inches without calling 811 in Florida?

Florida lets a single-family homeowner dig up to 10 inches on their own land without notice, using due care and staying out of utility easements. A call to Sunshine 811 is still the safer choice.

What color is a water line?

Water service pipe may be blue, black, white, gray or copper colored, depending on the material. Color alone isn't proof, so trace it before you cut.
